title: Chapter 141 – The War of Halls
html:
[Azure Cloud Sect – Head Wuping]

Wuping has been Head of the Azure Cloud Sect for forty-one years, and in all that time he has never once called a meeting he wanted to attend.

He calls this one for the morning after Ye's burial. The Hall of Assembly is cold. The braziers along the walls have been lit since dawn, but the room is too tall and too old to warm, and the breath of the sixty-two elders and hall-masters hangs over the long table like a second ceiling. He sits at the head of it in the plain gray robe of his office, with the jade seal on the cloth in front of him and his hands folded over it so that nobody will see them shake.

He has not slept. He has not slept since Ye's lamp went out. Every time he closes his eyes he sees the long banner of blank paper slipping down the nine steps of the Sutra Hall and coming to rest at Pei An's feet.

"We will begin," he says. His voice comes out thin. He clears his throat and tries again. "We will begin."

The room rustles and settles. At his right hand sits the Treasury Elder, Gu Mingzhe, a plump, soft-spoken man in a robe the color of old butter, with a ring on every finger. At his left, stiff and upright as a ruler, sits Law Elder Han, the woman who runs the Court. Beyond them are Pill Hall, the Weights, the Armory, the Grain Office, and the long benches of the lesser halls. Lu Fei, of the Hall of Weights, sits near the bottom, small and fierce and clutching a roll of readings against her chest like a shield. Of the Cloud Peak masters, only four have come. The rest are at their posts on the mountain, where Wuping told them to stay.

He lays out the matter in the plainest words he can find.

The Second House has served notice. By midwinter, in forty-three days, it will take the stair, the Dock, the Roll, and the title of Keeper. It will dissolve the Lin Seat. If the Sect refuses, it will come for them, not with swords, but with writs, with Registry seals, with the weight of six hundred years of paper and a hundred provincial offices that no longer answer to anyone in this room.

"And the Gate is failing," he finishes. "Lu Fei will tell you."

Lu Fei stands up. She is thirty-eight, and she has the look of a woman who has been awake for a week.

"The pulse of the lower Dock is down by two parts in three since spring," she says. "The stair is cold to the fifth landing. The Gate wall whispers at night. I have measured it eleven times." She swallows. "When Elder Ye finished the scroll, the pulse fell again. By a third of what was left. I do not know how long it will hold. A year. A season. I do not know."

Nobody speaks. Then Gu Mingzhe lifts one ringed hand, gently, as if asking permission to sneeze.

"Head Wuping. May I say something indelicate?"

"You may."

"The Treasury has never believed in the Dock." He smiles, apologetically. "Forgive me. It is not that I doubt it exists. I have seen the stair myself. It is only that the Treasury's business is the Sect's grain, and a thing that no one can sell, no one can count, and no one can use is, from a ledger's point of view, a liability." He spreads his hands. "The Second House has offered us a charter. The Sect keeps its lands and its mountain. It keeps its pill furnaces and its trade. In return, it asks only for the cellar under the Garden and some paper. I think we ought to accept."

There is a stir along the benches. Wuping feels his stomach turn over.

"The cellar under the Garden," he repeats, "is the Lin family's home."

"The Lin family is a very large family now," says Gu Mingzhe. "Four hundred and thirty people. It could be given other land. We are generous people."

Law Elder Han does not move. But she speaks, and her voice cuts the room like a blade through cloth.

"The Registry is an unlawful body."

"Elder Han—"

"I have the Articles in front of me. Forty-four and forty-five. No body outside the Sect may hold a Dock, a Roll or an oath of any pupil within the Sect's walls. None. Not the Second House, not the Court of the Weights, not the Throne." She taps the table. "The Treasury may sell its grain to whom it likes. But if it hands the Garden to the Registry, it hands them a pupil's oath. That is treason, and the Court will treat it as such."

"You would arrest the Treasury?"

"I would remind it."

The two of them glare at one another across the Head's seat like cats on a fence. Wuping, in between, sits with his hands over the seal and wishes, with the passionate sincerity of a man who has wished it every day for forty-one years, that he were somewhere else.

* * *

The meeting lasts four hours, and it ends in a vote that settles nothing.

By the end of it there are three parties. The Treasury and the Grain Office, eleven in all, would negotiate. The Court, the Armory and the Law benches, nineteen, would fight. The rest, thirty-two, will not be moved to either side and will say only that they are concerned. Pill Hall's master, a bald round man with a remarkably mild expression, declares that the Hall will remain neutral because pills are for everyone. Wuping thanks him with real warmth. It is the nicest thing anybody has said all day.

When the room has emptied, he sits on alone with his hands in his sleeves, looking at the seal.

He is a modest man. He knows it. He was chosen forty-one years ago because he was the one candidate whom no faction hated, and he has spent every year since being very careful not to become the one they hated. He has been agreeable. He has been quiet. When the Sect Head fell asleep in the Founders' Chamber seventy years ago and twenty-nine years of caretakers had come and gone, and the Head's seat passed to him, he took it in the spirit of a man given a vase to hold for a few minutes. It has been forty-one years. He has not put the vase down.

The door opens. Lu Fei comes in, still clutching her roll.

"Head. May I?"

"Please."

She sits across from him and unrolls her readings on the table, weighting the corners with his teacup and the seal and her own two fists. The ink lines run up and down in tiny, ragged peaks.

"I did not say everything in there," she says.

"I thought not."

"The pulse is falling. That is true. But look here." Her finger traces a line along the bottom of the page. "This is the Gate wall. Since the night Elder Ye finished, it has been making a different sound. Not a whisper. A kind of..." She searches for the word. "A kind of knocking."

"Knocking."

"As if someone were on the other side." She looks up, and he sees that she is frightened and ashamed of being frightened. "The old men in the east wing say it is Ye. They say she has gone through. I do not think it is Ye."

"What do you think it is?"

"I think the Gate is listening." She wets her lips. "I think it has been fed for six hundred years on names, and now the names are gone, and it is hungry. And I think the Second House knows it."

Wuping looks at the ragged lines. A cold feeling spreads slowly from the pit of his stomach to his fingertips.

"Who else has seen these?"

"You. Elder Jian."

"Not the Council."

"No."

"Keep it so," he says. He is surprised at his own voice. It is quiet and level. "For now."

* * *

The Garden of the Lin family lies two hours' walk from the Hall of Assembly, in the long green fold between Cloud Peak and the River Wei, and Wuping goes there on foot, without an escort, in the late afternoon.

He has not been in many years. It has changed. The old walled yard has become a village. There are rows of new tile roofs along the slope, a forge, a drying shed, a school where thirty children chant the Founders' sentence in a high ragged chorus, and an orchard of young apple trees in the lee of the wall. The people who pass him on the path stop and bow, and then, because they are Lins, they stare. They are a big, handsome, stubborn clan, and half of them have the same straight eyebrows.

Lin Wenyuan meets him at the gate.

He is eighty-five and looks sixty-five. Since the winter of his breakthrough his hands have been permanently cold, and he wears wool mittens in all weather, which makes him look like a very old child. But his back is straight and his grin is broad.

"Head Wuping," he says. "You look dreadful. Come in. Qinghe is making dumplings."

"I have come on business."

"Of course. Business can be done with dumplings."

It is a kitchen, a warm low room with a beam ceiling and a fire. Lin Qinghe stands at the table in her blue smock with flour to her elbows. She is eighty-two, sharp-eyed, small and fierce, and she has lost her sense of taste, which she has taken as a personal insult from heaven. She does not look up when Wuping enters. She says, "Sit," and he sits.

Lin Jian is at the far end of the table. He has been there some time. He is peeling an onion with a short knife, and the careful, absorbed way he does it tells Wuping that he is thinking about something else.

"I heard," says Jian. "The vote."

"Yes."

"Treasury is for taking the charter."

"Yes."

"And you?"

Wuping opens his mouth. Nothing comes out. He sits in the warm kitchen with the smell of onion and pork and wood-smoke, and a fire crackling in the hearth, and a hundred small domestic sounds going on around him, and finds that he cannot make himself say a word.

Qinghe puts down her rolling pin. She wipes her hands on her apron. She comes around the table and stands in front of him, and she looks down at him, a small gray woman with flour on her nose.

"Wuping," she says. "I knew your mother."

He blinks.

"She sold eggs by the east gate. She was a good woman and she was afraid of everything, and I was fond of her." Her mouth twitches. "You are exactly like her. You have been exactly like her for forty-one years. And I will tell you what she said to me, the week before she died. She said: I am tired of being careful. It has not made anyone safer."

The fire pops. Nobody speaks.

"Qinghe," murmurs Wenyuan.

"I am not finished." She does not take her eyes off Wuping. "My son will not ask you to fight. He is too polite. I am not. The Treasury would sell us for a bag of rice. The Court would use us for a banner. You are the Head. Be one."

Wuping looks down at his hands. They are long and thin and spotted with age. He has held a seal in them for forty-one years.

"If I side with you," he says slowly, "I lose the Treasury. The grain. The pills. The Sect's whole trade with the south. They will cut the Garden off. They will cut me off."

"Yes."

"The cost will be very great."

"Everything is," says Jian, without looking up from his onion. "I have found."

* * *

He goes back up the mountain in the dusk, and in the morning he does something that he has never done before.

He rings the Great Bell.

It hangs in the open tower above the Hall of Assembly, a cast bronze monster as tall as a man, and it has not been rung since the coronation of the last Emperor. Wuping pulls the rope himself, hand over hand, while two startled pupils stare. The sound rolls out over the mountain like thunder. All the way down the slopes, in every hall and bunkhouse, people stop what they are doing and lift their faces.

By noon the whole Sect is assembled in the court below the tower. Nine thousand pupils and disciples, in their blue and gray, standing in rows. The elders on the high steps. Gu Mingzhe in his butter-colored robe, with a face like a polite thundercloud. Law Elder Han behind him, arms folded. And at the head of it, small in his gray robe, with the jade seal in his hand and a sheet of paper in the other, the Head.

His knees feel like water. He starts to read. His voice cracks on the first line, and a few of the younger pupils smile, and he sees it and keeps going.

"This is the Head's order, in the sixty-fourth year of the Azure Cloud calendar. First. The Lin Seat is not dissolved. It is confirmed. It stands under Article Forty-four, and no body outside this Sect may touch it. Second. The Dock and the stair are the Sect's. They are not for sale or lease or charter. Third." He stops, because his throat has closed. He swallows. "Third. The Treasury will deliver the grain and the pills to the Garden on the usual schedule. Any Elder who refuses will answer to the Court."

A murmur runs through the rows.

"This is a lie," says Gu Mingzhe, quite pleasantly. "You cannot order the Treasury."

"I can."

"You are a caretaker. You have been one for forty years. The Sect will not follow you into a war with the Registry." He turns to the pupils with his ringed hands spread. "Children, I beg you. Think. The Registry holds the provincial offices. The salt. The ferries. The tax rolls of nine districts. If we make an enemy of them we will starve by spring."

It is true. Wuping can see the fear spreading across the court like a stain. A thousand faces shifting, a thousand small calculations. The Treasury Elder smiles. He knows it too.

Then, from the high steps, a clear voice rings out.

"Head. A moment."

It is Law Elder Han. She has taken one step forward. Her hand is on her sword, and for an instant Wuping thinks that this is the end, that she is going to arrest him, or cut him down, or demand the seal. Instead she draws the sword and drives it point-first into the stone.

"The Court of the Law stands with the Head," she says. "Under Article Forty-four. I will hold it against any hand."

* * *

The Sect does not fall into war that afternoon. It falls into something worse: a quarrel.

By evening the Treasury is shut, the Grain Office is shut, and a line of porters stands in the road outside both with their carrying poles on their shoulders, unsure whether they are on strike or on loan. A fight breaks out in the pill furnaces between two apprentices of rival halls. A caravan from the south, expected in three days, turns around at the border. Gu Mingzhe moves his family into the provincial office at Lower Weir, in a wagon train of twelve carts, and sends back a stiff, polite note that begins With deep regret.

Wuping reads it in his office at midnight, by one candle. He has been reading things for forty-one years, and this is the first one that has ever made him laugh.

He laughs until his sides hurt. Then he puts his head down on the desk and cries a little, quietly, with the sleeve of his robe pressed against his mouth. He is seventy. He has just done the bravest thing of his life and lost half of everything he has, and he is horribly, helplessly happy.

When he looks up, a man is standing in the door.

It is not a pupil. It is Pei An of the Second House, bearded and tired in his plain gray tunic, with no satchel this time, and no seal. His eyes are red. He has the look of someone who has walked a long way in the dark.

"Head Wuping," he says. "I am sorry. Your guards let me in. I told them I came to surrender."

"To surrender."

"Yes." Pei An's mouth works. "Or not exactly. I have not been to the Warden. I do not think I can go back to him." He holds out his empty hands. "I have eleven names on Ye's scroll. I heard each one read. I have not slept since. I have come to ask what a man does who has done what I have done."

Wuping stares at him. The candle gutters. In the long quiet he feels the world turn on its axis, slowly, with a sound like a door swinging on a hinge.

"Sit down," he says. "I do not know what a man does. But I have tea. And I have found, lately, that it helps to begin with tea."

Pei An sits. His shoulders shake.

"There are a hundred and sixty of us," he says. "In the old Registry hall at Lower Weir. Clerks. Men who burned names. Most of us were at the steps that night. The Warden says that Ye's reading was a trick. That it was meant to break the House. He has doubled the guard on the lower stair. He means to take it by force, on the new moon, before midwinter." He draws a breath. "I thought you should know."

"Why tell me?"

"Because I wanted," says Pei An slowly, "to be someone who told."

Wuping pours the tea. His hand is steady. It is the first time all day that it has been.

* * *

They hold the Garden gate against the first attempt, on the night of the new moon.

It is not much of a battle. It is a long cold hour on a dark ridge, with torches guttering in the wind, and two hundred men in plum-trimmed gray coming up the road from Lower Weir in a column, and three hundred Lins and Sect pupils standing in a line along the wall with Law Elder Han's sword in the middle of it like a post. Wenyuan is there, in his mittens, with an apple-wood staff. Qinghe is there, with a kitchen knife that she has been sharpening since dusk. Jian stands at the center of the gate, in his brown cloak, with his eyes half closed, and Wuping, who has come against all advice, stands behind him, clutching the jade seal in both hands like a man holding a lantern in a flood.

The column stops at forty paces.

At its head walks a tall man in the Warden's gray. Shen Yuhang. Golden Core. He has changed. His face has gone smooth and sleek, the face of a man who has spent too long looking at a ledger, and his eyes are very pale. He lifts one hand and the column halts.

"Head Wuping," he says. His voice carries without effort. "I am sorry for this. Truly. You have no idea what you are defending."

"I have some idea."

"You do not." The Warden smiles. "Open the gate. Give me the stair. I will leave the Sect its mountain. I will leave you your seal. I do not want a war. I want only to keep the Chain from breaking."

"And the sleepers?"

"They will be kept."

"As fuel."

Something flickers in the pale eyes. For a moment, the smile is gone.

"As long as is necessary," says Shen Yuhang. "That is all I will say."

Jian steps forward.

He does it quietly, with no flourish. He walks ten paces down the road and stops in the middle of it with his hands loose at his sides, and the Warden's column goes still. Nobody moves. The torches hiss.

"You are afraid," Jian says. His voice is mild. "I understand that. I am afraid too. But I will tell you what I told you on the steps. There is another way, and it does not run through the stair. Give me until midwinter. If I fail, you can take your writs and your charters and do as you like."

"You have nothing to bargain with."

"I have forty-one days." He shrugs. "And a hundred and sixty clerks who have just heard their own names."

It is a guess. Wuping sees it, from where he stands: sees the faint tightening of the Warden's mouth, and the movement in the ranks behind him, the quick glances, the men in the front rows looking at their shoes. Pei An is in that column. He is in the sixth rank, with his hands empty. As Wuping watches, he steps out of line, walks the length of the column, and stops beside Jian.

"I will stay here," he says, in a clear shaking voice. "If the Warden wishes to take the stair, he may begin with me."

A second man follows him. Then a woman. Then four. Then fifty. They come out of the ranks one by one and cross the forty paces of frozen road, and stand in the torchlight in their plum-trimmed gray, and do not look back.

Shen Yuhang looks at them for a long time. He does not raise his hand again.

"Midwinter," he says at last. His voice is dry as paper. "Not one day more."

He turns. The column goes with him, ragged now, a hundred men instead of two. The sound of their boots fades down the dark road toward Lower Weir.

Wuping realizes that he is crying again. He does not wipe his face.

"That was a gamble," he says hoarsely.

"Yes," says Jian.

"You did not know they would come over."

"No." He turns, and for the first time in years Wuping sees him smile, a quick tired boyish smile that has nothing of the Purple Mansion in it at all. "But Ye did. I think she spent twenty-four years making sure."

* * *

They bury Ye's stick the next day, in the Garden orchard, under a young apple tree.

It is a small ceremony. Perhaps a thousand people come. There are the Lins, the pupils, the restored from the east wing in their borrowed tunics, Pei Wanli with his noodle wife and the two small Wanlings, and a new man at the back, tall and broad, with a scar through his left eyebrow, who stands apart with his face lifted to the sky and does not seem to hear anything anyone says. Ning Ruiyan is counting stars in the daylight. Nobody tries to stop him.

Wuping stands at the graveside, small and gray, with the seal in his sleeve. He has not been a good Head. He has been a careful one. Today, for the first time, he thinks that perhaps those are not entirely different things.

Lu Fei finds him as the crowd begins to leave. She has her roll under her arm. Her face is the color of chalk.

"Head. I took another reading this morning."

"And?"

"The knocking has stopped."

He feels his heart go still.

"That is good, surely."

"No." She shakes her head. "It does not stop on its own. I checked the old Weights tables. In six hundred years it has stopped only once. On the night of the First Sleeper." She holds out the sheet. In the middle of the ragged peaks, a single clean line runs straight across the page, flat as a ruled edge. "It is not hungry anymore, Head. It has been fed."

"By whom?"

"I do not know. But Head..." Her voice drops. "The stair is warm. All the way down. For the first time in forty years."

Wuping looks at the paper. Then he looks across the orchard, to where Jian stands alone at the edge of the grave with his head bowed and his hand resting on the bark of the new tree.

Somewhere far underground, in the deep dark, something very old has opened an eye.
